content.text: The compass needle stuttered near the iron ridge, and my father wrote iron ridge suspected in a hand that did not stutter. A room remembers its last occupant longer than most people expect. The kettle took its usual three minutes, and in that time the whole morning seemed to settle.

A map left unfinished is a kind of promise, and I have tried, since his death, to keep it. Distance is measured in more than miles once you have walked enough of it yourself. A garden left untended for a season still remembers, mostly, what it was planted to become.

Notes toward a new coastline filled the last notebook, in handwriting that grew smaller as the ink ran low. The clock in the hall ran two minutes fast for as long as anyone could remember, and no one corrected it. Patience is easier to recommend than to practise, a fact every teacher of it eventually admits.

The survey crew joked that the mountains resented being measured, and after enough seasons I half agreed with them. The correspondence between old friends thins with distance but rarely stops outright. A machine well maintained will forgive a great many small mistakes; one neglected forgives none.

Every triangulation point was a small stone cairn, and every cairn was, in its way, a signature. Quiet, in the right house, is not an absence of sound but a particular kind of company. The weather that season did exactly what the almanac predicted, which surprised everyone involved.

I have walked the unfinished edge myself now, twice, and both times turned back before I could finish it either. A long walk clarifies more than a long conversation, in my limited experience of both. The light in late afternoon has a habit of making ordinary rooms look briefly important.

The map is still wrong in the same stubborn margin, and I have decided, for now, to let it be wrong honestly. Memory keeps the details it wants and discards the ones it decides, later, were never essential. A well-kept ledger tells you less about money than it does about the person who kept it.

The map was unfinished at the eastern ridge, which is another way of saying the ridge was unfinished with us. The city at that hour belonged mostly to delivery carts and the occasional insomniac. Old letters, reread, always sound slightly more confident than the person who wrote them actually was.

My father surveyed by day and redrew his own errors by lamplight, muttering that the land moved more than it ought. A door left ajar in an old house creaks in a key entirely its own. The harvest that year came in later than usual, and no less welcome for it.

There are rivers on no map I have ever seen, not because no one has found them but because no one has agreed on their name. Silence between two people who know each other well is rarely uncomfortable. The workshop light stayed on past midnight more nights than either of us cared to count.

The instrument case held a theodolite older than either of us, its brass gone the colour of weak tea. A path worn into a lawn tells you exactly where people actually wanted the path to be. The sea keeps no calendar, which is either its great honesty or its great indifference.

We measured the coastline twice that season, and it disagreed with itself both times by the same stubborn margin. An old friend visiting after years away brings the past with them, uninvited but not unwelcome. The bread was better that winter, though no one could say exactly why.

A cartographer's daughter learns early that the map is not the country, only an argument in favour of one. A long apprenticeship teaches humility faster than it teaches skill, and in the correct order. The train timetable was more aspiration than fact, and everyone along the line understood as much.

Where the survey chain would not reach, my father estimated, and where he estimated, he wrote it plainly on the page. A candle burns down evenly only if you trim the wick, a lesson repeated in every household. The orchard gave less fruit that year but of a better, denser sweetness.

The ridge kept its own weather, sending down fog long after the valley below had cleared entirely. A stranger's kindness on a hard day is remembered longer than most kindnesses from family. The wind off the water carried salt far enough inland to whiten the window glass by spring.

I have inherited the case, the instruments, and the habit of distrusting any coastline drawn too confidently. A journal kept honestly becomes, without meaning to, a kind of second memory. The market emptied by four, leaving only the smell of what had been sold there.

A new edge of the map is never blank so much as honest about what has not yet been walked. An old dog knows the sound of the right footsteps long before anyone else in the house does. The harvest moon that year hung low enough to seem, briefly, close.

The eastern survey took eleven weeks and produced four pages, which my father considered a fair exchange. A debt repaid on time is remembered less than one repaid a day late. The workshop smelled of sawdust and, faintly, of the coffee no one ever finished.

Rivers move, he used to say, and so does the truth, and a good map only ever catches one of them resting. A letter that arrives too late still says something true, even if the moment has passed. The garden wall held the day's heat long after the sun itself had gone down.

We named the smaller creek for my mother, since no one else had claimed it and she deserved a river. An empty house is loud in a way a full one never manages to be. The apprentice years pass slowly at the time and quickly in the remembering.

A well-worn tool fits the hand better than any new one, however well made. The evening train was always half empty, and always exactly on time. An old photograph tells you what a person looked like and almost nothing about who they were.

The bakery opened before the rest of the street had decided the day had begun. A long correspondence, kept up faithfully, is its own kind of small monument. The frost came early that year and stripped the orchard almost overnight.

An honest account of a hard season reads, afterward, like a much easier one than it was. The workshop door stuck in wet weather, a fault no one ever quite got around to fixing. A river town keeps different hours than a market town, and neither much minds the other's.

The last light of the day fell across the table in a way that made finishing supper feel unhurried. An old coat, kept for sentiment, still fits better than most people expect. The harbor quieted by evening to the sound of ropes against the pilings and little else.

A neighbor's lamp, lit before dawn, was as good as a clock to anyone passing. The season turned the way seasons do, without asking anyone's permission first. An unfinished letter is, in its way, more honest than a finished one.

The workshop ledger recorded debts in pencil and settlements in ink, and rarely confused the two. A well-worn path through a wood is a kind of quiet agreement among everyone who uses it. The morning fog burned off by nine most days, later on the days it mattered least.
